motivation: In 1979 Tajima (with the late John Dawson) proposed that an intense laser pulse in a plasma drives a wake whose electric fields exceed those of conventional radiofrequency accelerators by three orders of magnitude. Once ultrashort, ultra-intense pulses became available, experimentalists turned that idea into a real accelerator. In 2004 groups led by Malka at LOA and Leemans at Berkeley, together with a UK team, produced quasi-monoenergetic electron beams. Leemans's group later reached multi-GeV energies over centimetres, and Malka's group developed controlled injection and applications. The work set up a new field in physics: compact accelerators, betatron and Compton X-ray sources, and a credible path to plasma-driven free-electron lasers and future colliders. It is a fundamental plasma-physics discovery carried through by persistent, difficult laboratory work, and it deserves recognition.
